title: Koin & DI Alternatives
scopeHtml: Koin (runtime DSL), kotlin-inject, Anvil/Metro, and the Hilt vs Koin vs manual DI trade-offs. Version notes come from the Koin docs (4.2.x line at time of research) and the Metro docs; anything marked "verify" must be re-checked before you quote it.

questions.promptHtml: What is Koin, and how does it differ mechanically from Dagger/Hilt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the compile-time vs runtime resolution split, which drives every other trade-off.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Koin is a Kotlin DSL-based DI library. You declare definitions in module { } blocks, startKoin registers them in a container, and dependencies are resolved at runtime by looking up the type in that container. Dagger/Hilt generates Java/Kotlin code at build time and validates the whole graph then. So Koin is easy and fast to build, but a missing binding is a runtime exception, not a build error, unless you add verification.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Koin keeps a registry (Koin instance, holding a Scope/InstanceRegistry) mapping a type (plus optional qualifier) to a definition lambda. get<T>() looks up the definition and invokes the lambda, which itself calls get() for its constructor args. No code generation, no annotation processing, no reflection in the common path (definitions are lambdas; singleOf(::Foo) uses a function reference).

Dagger/Hilt:  build time  -> graph validated -> generated Factory classes -> runtime just calls them
Koin (DSL):   runtime     -> registry lookup by type -> lambda invoked -> exception if missing

Consequences: no kapt/KSP cost, tiny build impact, easy KMP support; but graph correctness is only proven when a path executes (or in a verification test).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val appModule = module {
    single<UserRepository> { UserRepositoryImpl(get(), get()) }
    factory { FormatUseCase(get()) }
    viewModelOf(::ProfileViewModel)
}

class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        startKoin {
            androidContext(this@App)
            modules(appModule)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Koin is not DI, it is a service locator". It is DI when you constructor-inject via the DSL, and a locator when you call get()/inject() from your own classes. Be precise.
  • Claiming Koin has "no compile-time safety" without mentioning verify() and the Koin compiler plugin (see Q232, Q235).
  • Calling startKoin twice (e.g., in tests or multiple processes) causes KoinAppAlreadyStartedException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Koin use reflection? -> Not for the DSL path; definitions are lambdas. Reflection was only in some older/get<T>() class-name keying (it uses KClass).
  2. Where does the container live? -> A global GlobalContext by default; you can run an isolated koinApplication { } for tests/libraries.
  3. What happens in a multi-process app? -> Each process has its own Application.onCreate and its own container; you must start Koin per process, and singletons are per process.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Koin is simpler, Hilt is safer." Senior: explains registry-based resolution, where failures surface (first resolution of that path), and that safety is recoverable through verify() or the compiler plugin.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rarely-visited screen crashed in production with NoDefinitionFoundException after a refactor because nothing resolved its ViewModel in CI.

questions.promptHtml: Explain single, factory, viewModel and the *Of constructor DSL in Koin. When would each be wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Instance lifetime is the root of most Koin bugs (stale state, leaks).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: single creates one instance for the container's lifetime, factory creates a new one on every request, viewModel creates one per ViewModel store owner (it hooks into ViewModelProvider). The singleOf(::Foo) forms are shorthand that resolve constructor params with get(). Wrong choices: single for anything holding per-screen or per-user state, factory for something expensive or something that must be shared.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• single: lazy by default (created on first resolution) unless createdAtStart = true.
  • factory: new instance per get(); no lifecycle, Koin does not track it, so you own cleanup.
  • viewModel/viewModelOf: registered so koinViewModel() or by viewModel() obtains it through the platform's ViewModelProvider, so it survives configuration change and is cleared with its owner. Resolving it with plain get() outside a ViewModelStore gives you a non-lifecycle-managed instance (a classic bug).
  • scoped: one per Koin scope instance (see Q231).
  • bind/binds: singleOf(::RepoImpl) { bind<Repo>() } exposes an interface.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val dataModule = module {
    singleOf(::RepoImpl) { bind<Repo>() }          // shared, exposed as interface
    factoryOf(::DateFormatter)                      // cheap, stateless: fine either way
}
val uiModule = module {
    viewModelOf(::ProfileViewModel)                 // per owner via ViewModelProvider
}

@Composable
fun ProfileRoute() {
    val vm: ProfileViewModel = koinViewModel()     // not get<ProfileViewModel>()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• single { ShoppingCartHolder() } for per-user state: survives logout.
  • get<MyViewModel>() in an Activity: bypasses the store, rotation recreates it.
  • Assuming createdAtStart is free: it moves cost to cold start.
  • Using the *Of DSL with a constructor that has default params or nullable/ambiguous types, which can resolve wrongly or fail at runtime.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. single vs Kotlin object? -> single is replaceable in tests and has a container-controlled lifecycle.
  2. How do you pass runtime args? -> parametersOf(...) and getKoin().get { parametersOf(id) }, or koinViewModel { parametersOf(id) }.
  3. How do you avoid circular deps? -> Koin will stack overflow/throw at resolution; restructure, or inject Lazy via inject().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the keywords. Senior ties each to a lifetime and names the failure when it is mismatched, plus the viewModel-resolved-via-get trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "single" holding a search filter made filters persist after logout and leak across accounts.

questions.promptHtml: How do Koin scopes work, and how do they compare to Hilt component scopes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Scoping is where DI frameworks differ most and where logout/account bugs live.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Koin scope is a runtime container you create and close manually (or tie to a lifecycle), holding scoped definitions declared in a scope<T> / scope(named(...)) section. scoped instances live until that scope instance is closed. Hilt's scopes are fixed, generated components tied to Android lifecycles; Koin's are open-ended and dynamic, so per-user or per-flow scopes are easy, but you own correct closing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declare: scope<UserSession> { scoped { Cart() } } or scope(named("user")) { }.
  • Create: koin.createScope(id, named("user")). Resolve: scope.get<Cart>().
  • Close: scope.close() runs onClose callbacks, releases instances; later get() throws ClosedScopeException. At logout: koin.getScopeOrNull(userId)?.close().
  • A scope can resolve definitions from the root (single) but root definitions cannot depend on scoped ones (no upward references, they would outlive the scope).
  • Android helpers (activity/fragment scopes, viewModelScope archetype) exist; the ViewModel scope API is marked experimental in the docs, so verify before relying on it.
Hilt:  SingletonComponent > ActivityRetainedComponent > ViewModelComponent ...  (fixed, generated)
Koin:  root Koin  > any number of named/typed Scope instances you create/close (dynamic)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val sessionModule = module {
    scope<UserSession> {
        scoped { CartStore(get<UserSession>().userId) }
    }
}

fun onLogin(koin: Koin, userId: String): Scope =
    koin.createScope(userId, named<UserSession>())

fun onLogout(koin: Koin, userId: String) {
    koin.getScopeOrNull(userId)?.close()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding a reference to a scoped instance in a root single after the scope closed (a leak plus stale object).
  • Forgetting to close: the scope id is registered globally; creating the same id twice throws.
  • Assuming a scope auto-closes without a lifecycle owner binding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you do per-user DI in Hilt? -> Custom component with @DefineComponent, or a manually built holder; more ceremony (see session chunk).
  2. What is ClosedScopeException telling you? -> Something outlived its scope, a lifecycle bug in your code.
  3. Can scopes be tested? -> Yes, create/close in test and assert resolution fails after close.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "scopes limit lifetime." Senior: contrasts dynamic vs generated, calls out ownership of close(), and the no-upward-dependency rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Account switching served the previous user's data until a scope was keyed by user id and closed on logout.

questions.promptHtml: Koin resolves at runtime. How do you stop a missing definition from reaching production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you mitigate the main Koin weakness with real tooling rather than opinion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Three layers: a unit test calling module.verify() (from org.koin.test.verify) that statically checks constructor dependencies are declared; an integration test that actually starts Koin with real modules and resolves the key entry points; and optionally the Koin compiler plugin, which moves the check to build time. I'd also run a launch smoke test per ViewModel in CI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• verify() inspects definitions' constructor parameter types via reflection on the JVM and checks a matching definition exists. It does not execute the lambdas. It needs extraTypes for types provided at runtime (e.g., Context, SavedStateHandle, parametersOf args).
  • Limits: it checks declared constructor types, not custom get() calls inside lambda bodies (e.g., single { Foo(get("x")) } with qualifiers/params it cannot see), so lambda-style definitions are weaker than *Of.
  • checkModules is the older API (verify, in current docs).
  • The compiler plugin (Koin 4.x line, labelled experimental in the releases page at time of research, verify) reports missing dependencies during compilation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ModulesCheckTest {
    @OptIn(KoinExperimentalAPI::class)
    @Test
    fun verifyAppModules() {
        appModule.verify(
            extraTypes = listOf(Context::class, SavedStateHandle::class)
        )
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• A green verify() treated as proof; it can miss qualifier and parameter issues.
  • Never running the test in CI because it is "just a unit test".
  • Verifying only one module while the real graph merges several; verify what ships.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can verify miss things? -> It cannot see inside lambdas; only declared types.
  2. How else would you catch it? -> Instrumented smoke test that navigates/instantiates each ViewModel.
  3. Does the compiler plugin make Koin equal to Hilt? -> Closer on missing bindings; Hilt still validates scope and cycle rules and gives full dependency-path errors, and the plugin's maturity needs verifying.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "write a test." Senior: knows what the test cannot detect, adds smoke tests, and evaluates build-time options with a maturity caveat.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: NoDefinitionFoundException on a deep-link-only screen shipped because only home screens were exercised in tests.

questions.promptHtml: Is Koin a service locator? Why do people say service locators are bad, and how do you use Koin without becoming one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core DI design principle: dependencies visible in constructors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The pattern is a service locator when a class pulls its own dependencies from a global container (by inject(), get(), KoinComponent). That hides dependencies, makes tests need a global container, and fails at runtime. Koin is DI when you only use it at the composition root: definitions pass dependencies through constructors, and classes never know Koin exists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problems with locator use: hidden dependencies (constructor lies), global mutable state shared across tests, harder static analysis, tight coupling to the framework in domain code. Koin supports both styles; the documentation even lists injecting from outside as a Android-entry-point necessity (Activities, Services you do not construct).

// Locator style (avoid in domain/data code)
class Repo : KoinComponent { private val api: Api by inject() }

// DI style
class Repo(private val api: Api)
val m = module { singleOf(::Repo) }

Allowed pragmatic use of inject()/koinViewModel(): Android framework entry points (Activity, Application, Compose route functions). Keep it at the edge.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• KoinComponent in repositories and use cases.
  • Using get() inside a ViewModel body lazily to dodge a cycle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Hilt @EntryPoint a locator? -> Partly yes; it is the sanctioned escape hatch for non-injectable classes.
  2. How to unit test a KoinComponent? -> Needs startKoin/KoinTestRule; a constructor class needs nothing.
  3. Can you ban it? -> Lint/Konsist rule forbidding KoinComponent outside *Application/UI packages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior separates the pattern from the library and enforces the rule mechanically.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A test suite became order-dependent because a class used a global inject() and a prior test left Koin started.

questions.subtopic: Hilt vs Koin vs manual DI
questions.promptHtml: Compare Hilt, Koin and manual DI. How do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic "justify your choice" question; seniors answer with criteria, not tribal preference.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hilt gives build-time graph validation, Android lifecycle scopes and first-party support, at the cost of kapt/KSP build time and Android-only. Koin gives a tiny learning curve, no codegen and KMP support, but runtime failures unless verified. Manual DI gives zero framework and full control, but you hand-write the wiring and scoping. I choose by team size, build pain, KMP needs and how costly a runtime wiring failure is.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Criterion Hilt Koin Manual
Missing binding build error runtime (or verify / compiler plugin) compile error (it is just code)
Build cost annotation processing none for DSL none
KMP Android only yes yes
Scopes fixed Android components dynamic, manual close you write holders
Learning curve steep errors gentle none, but boilerplate grows
Startup generated factories; lazy registers definitions at start depends

Startup claims are contested between vendor and community posts. I would not quote numbers; I would benchmark with Macrobenchmark on a mid-range device (verify on your own app).

Manual DI (an AppContainer plus per-feature containers) is fully viable below ~15-20 screens; it breaks down when scoping and ordering rules multiply.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring a winner by startup micro-benchmarks from a blog.
  • Ignoring the team: a rotating team of juniors gets more value from compile-time errors.
  • Forgetting KMP: Hilt cannot live in commonMain.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Startup 800 ms to 1.1 s: is DI the cause? -> Profile first (Perfetto/Macrobenchmark); eager singletons and createdAtStart are likelier culprits than the framework.
  2. KMP app today? -> Koin or Metro/kotlin-inject in common code; Hilt can stay Android-side only.
  3. Can you mix? -> Yes, e.g., Hilt on Android and Koin shared module bridged via a provided interface, at a cost of two mental models.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average ranks by popularity. Senior gives decision criteria and states what evidence would change the decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team picked Koin for speed and later added verification tests plus smoke tests after two wiring crashes.

questions.promptHtml: What are Koin Annotations and the Koin compiler plugin, and does either change the Hilt-vs-Koin argument?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks currency; most Koin criticisms are outdated.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Koin Annotations (@Single, @Factory, @KoinViewModel, @Module) generate the DSL definitions at build time through KSP, so you get declarative style and some compile-time checks. The newer Koin compiler plugin, per the Koin docs, runs inside Kotlin compilation, supports DSL and annotations, and turns a missing dependency into a build error; the KSP processor is being deprecated in its favour. It narrows the safety gap with Hilt, but the plugin is labelled experimental in the releases page, so I would verify its status before adopting it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Annotation modes: you still end with the same runtime registry; the generated code is module { } definitions.
  • Compile safety in annotations mode: can detect missing deps, with KSP configuration options (KOIN_CONFIG_CHECK-style flags; verify exact names).
  • Plugin benefits: no KSP step, KMP without per-target KSP wiring.
  • Remaining differences: Hilt validates scope compatibility, entry points and gives full dependency-path errors; Koin runtime semantics (dynamic scopes, parameters, getKoin()) are looser by design.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Single
class UserRepositoryImpl(private val api: UserApi) : UserRepository

@KoinViewModel
class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: UserRepository) : ViewModel()

@Module
@ComponentScan("com.example.app")
class AppModule

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating annotations as "now it is Dagger". Resolution is still runtime, errors differ.
  • Mixing KSP processor and compiler plugin in the same module.
  • Upgrading Kotlin without checking plugin compatibility (compiler plugins are tied to compiler versions).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are compiler plugins version-fragile? -> They use compiler internals (FIR/IR); each Kotlin release can break them.
  2. Does annotation mode add build time? -> KSP is cheaper than kapt but not free; the plugin removes that step (verify measurements).
  3. Would you adopt an experimental plugin in prod? -> Behind a verified CI and a rollback path (keep DSL definitions working).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior tracks ecosystem direction and treats "experimental" as a risk to price, not a blocker or a green light.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Kotlin upgrade blocked for two weeks because a third-party compiler plugin lagged behind the compiler release.

questions.contextHtml:
A marketplace app (2M DAU, Koin 3.5) has a bug report: users see the previous search's filters when opening search again, and after logout/login as another account, the cart briefly shows the old user's items. Crash rate is flat (0.3%). Code:

val appModule = module {
    single { SearchFilterHolder() }          // holds MutableStateFlow<Filters>
    single { CartRepository(get()) }
    single { ProfileViewModel(get()) }
}
class ProfileActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: ProfileViewModel by inject()
}

Rotation on the profile screen also shows stale scroll state and the screen keeps updating after it is closed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use factory everywhere." Ignores that the cart legitimately needs sharing and that the ViewModel bug is about the owner, not the lifetime keyword.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the filter meant to survive within a session? Is there a logout hook? Is ProfileViewModel expected to be per screen? Does anything else observe the cart?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that clears the holder and cart in the logout path; behind a flag if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) single for state that has a shorter lifetime than the process; (b) ViewModel registered as single and obtained via inject(), so it is not owned by a ViewModelStore; (c) cart tied to no user scope; (d) red herring: rotation is unrelated to Koin graph.
  4. How I'd verify: Log identity hash of the instances across logout; heap dump / LeakCanary showing the Activity retained through a single ViewModel; unit test resolving twice.
  5. Root cause: A single ViewModel is a process-wide object: never cleared, and it can hold Activity-derived references and keep its collectors alive. The filter holder and cart have user/session lifetime but process lifetime in DI.
  6. Fix: short term: viewModelOf(::ProfileViewModel) with by viewModel(); reset on logout. Long term: user scope.
val appModule = module {
    single { SearchFilterHolder() }                       // only if filters outlive screens
    viewModelOf(::ProfileViewModel)
    scope<UserSession> { scoped { CartRepository(get()) } }
}
// logout: koin.getScopeOrNull(userId)?.close()
  1. Prevention: Konsist/lint rule: no ViewModel subclass in single; session-state review checklist; integration test: login A, add to cart, logout, login B, assert empty.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not make everything factory, it breaks legitimate sharing. Not add manual reset calls scattered around; scope closing is one place.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the cart must survive process death? -> Persist it (database); scope only governs in-memory lifetime.
  • What if a background worker needs the cart? -> Resolve through the user scope's id, handle the "no session" case explicitly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found a singleton ViewModel holding a destroyed Activity's context; the symptom was a slow memory climb and two-user data bleed, found only via a heap dump.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps single for factory blindly.
  • Hire: fixes ViewModel registration and identifies session-state lifetime.
  • Strong hire: introduces a user scope with close-on-logout, a regression test and a lint guard.

questions.promptHtml: What is kotlin-inject, how does it work, and how does it differ from Dagger and Koin?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes awareness of compile-time DI designed for Kotlin and KMP.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: kotlin-inject is a compile-time DI library (KSP-based) with a Dagger-like annotation model but a Kotlin-first design: you define a @Component as an abstract class or interface and it generates the implementation. Like Dagger it validates the graph at build time; unlike Dagger it works in Kotlin Multiplatform, and it supports constructor default arguments and function injection. Compared with Koin, you get compile-time safety, at the cost of KSP processing and fewer ready-made Android integrations.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Components are declared by you, and the generated class (InjectAppComponent) is created with a generated create() extension.
  • Scopes are custom annotations marked @Scope and applied on component and provider.
  • Provider methods live in component interfaces (@Provides functions or properties), supporting composition by interface inheritance.
  • Missing binding is a compile error naming the type.
  • Anvil-style contribution aggregation (@ContributesTo, @ContributesBinding) is provided by a separate library, kotlin-inject-anvil, for multi-module graphs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Scope annotation class AppScope

@Inject @AppScope
class UserRepository(private val api: UserApi)

@Component @AppScope
abstract class AppComponent {
    @Provides fun api(): UserApi = UserApiImpl()
    abstract val repo: UserRepository
}

val component = AppComponent::class.create()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Hilt-style Android integration (no @AndroidEntryPoint; you wire ViewModels yourself).
  • Assuming multi-module aggregation is built in.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Dagger in KMP? -> Dagger is JVM/Java-annotation based, so common code cannot use it.
  2. Biggest practical pain? -> ViewModel/Navigation integration is manual; ecosystem size.
  3. How does it compare to Metro? -> Metro (compiler plugin) draws on kotlin-inject's interface-based graphs plus Anvil-style aggregation and Dagger's annotations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can place it on the spectrum: runtime-DSL (Koin) <-> compile-time Kotlin-native (kotlin-inject, Metro) <-> compile-time JVM (Dagger/Hilt).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: KMP teams adopted it when needing both safety and shared DI code in commonMain.

questions.promptHtml: What problem did Anvil solve, and where do Metro and kotlin-inject-anvil fit in today's DI landscape? What is the status?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Staff-level awareness of modular DI aggregation and of what to bet on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Anvil (by Square, since archived/superseded for many; verify) added @ContributesTo/@ContributesBinding-style aggregation so modules contribute bindings to a scope without a central module listing them, which helps multi-module and build time. Metro is a newer compiler-plugin DI framework by Zac Sweers that combines Dagger-style annotations, kotlin-inject-style interface graphs and Anvil-style aggregation, with KMP support and no KAPT/KSP. I would evaluate it as promising and track its maturity (verify current release and Hilt interop status) before betting a large app on it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Why aggregation matters: in a many-module app, a central @Module(includes=...) list couples the app module to every feature. Contributions invert that: the feature declares itself; the graph assembles at the app module.
  • Metro (per its docs): compiler-plugin (FIR/IR) implementation; supports JVM, Android, JS, Wasm, Native; offers Dagger and kotlin-inject interop for component-level migration.
  • Amazon's App Platform docs recommend Metro as the default and keep kotlin-inject-anvil as an alternative for existing code.
  • Risk: compiler plugins track Kotlin versions; community-driven projects have bus-factor risk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Metro-style (illustrative; verify annotation names against current docs)
@DependencyGraph(AppScope::class)
interface AppGraph {
    val repo: UserRepository
}

@ContributesBinding(AppScope::class)
class RealUserRepository @Inject constructor(api: UserApi) : UserRepository

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Presenting Metro as "the new standard"; it is one option and Google still endorses Hilt for Android.
  • Ignoring Kotlin version coupling.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Hilt equivalent of aggregation? -> @InstallIn modules discovered via the Hilt aggregating Gradle task; no manual list, but Android-only.
  2. Migration path? -> Metro documents interop so a graph can depend on Dagger/kotlin-inject components, enabling incremental module-by-module migration.
  3. What would make you adopt? -> KMP need, build-time evidence, active maintenance and a rollback path.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior frames it as aggregation + KMP + compiler-plugin trade-offs and states the adoption criteria.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams with 100+ modules cited the central module list as a merge-conflict hot spot that contribution annotations removed.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (800k DAU, Koin 4.0) had an incident: after "Switch account", about 0.4% of sessions (roughly 3k users/day) saw the previous account's balance for 1-3 seconds, and 30 reports of a transfer screen prefilled with another account's payee. No crashes. Releases: the account-switch feature shipped 2 weeks ago. Code review shows scope(named("user")) exists, but account switch calls createScope(userId) for the new user and closes the old scope only on explicit logout. Network is fine; the delay correlates with slow devices.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: root cause, fix, prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames caching or the network; proposes "just clear the UI". Never examines instance lifetime.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are flows collected by long-lived singletons? Which components hold references to the old scope? Is the account id part of every repository key? Is there an ordering between close and create?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server flag to disable account switch (or force full relaunch on switch) while fixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) old scope not closed on switch, still serving; (b) root single caching a scoped instance reference captured at first resolution; (c) collectors in ViewModels that survive and were bound to the old scope; (d) red herring: network latency, which only widens the visible window on slow devices.
  4. How I'd verify: Log scope ids at create/close; call getScopeOrNull(oldId), expecting null after switch; heap dump to find who retains the old CartStore/BalanceRepository; reproduce with a throttled device and instrumented test.
  5. Root cause: Scope lifecycle tied to logout only; account switch created a second live scope while a root-level holder (the "current session" singleton) still resolved the previous one until the new data arrived. Stale reads persisted until a refresh overwrote them.
  6. Fix: One SessionManager owns transitions: close old scope, create new, publish StateFlow<SessionScope?>, ViewModels derive from that flow.
suspend fun switchTo(newId: String) {
    current?.close()                       // close first
    current = koin.createScope(newId, named("user"))
    _session.value = newId
}

Make repositories keyed by user id and clear in-flight jobs on close. 7. Prevention: instrumented test for A->B switch with a fake slow network; a rule that scoped instances must never be stored in root singletons; alerts on ClosedScopeException rate and a client-side invariant log (userId on response vs session). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on UI-level clearing; not skip the SessionManager and sprinkle closes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a Worker is running during the switch? -> Tag work with user id; cancel/ignore on mismatch.
  • Would Hilt have prevented it? -> Not automatically; a custom component would encode the lifetime but the transition logic is still yours.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found the "current user" singleton lazily captured the first scope; the fix was making session a flow, not a captured reference.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: UI clearing or cache blame.
  • Hire: scope close/create ordering and root cause.
  • Strong hire: SessionManager, invariants, user-keyed repositories and a prevention test suite.

questions.contextHtml: You are the first Android hire at a 12-person startup (a single Android app, 14 screens, 3 Android engineers soon, iOS app in Swift, KMP discussed but not committed). The CTO asks which DI approach to use. The current code uses manual singletons. Cold start is 1.9 s p50 on mid-range devices; the CI build is 6 min.
questions.promptHtml: What do you pick and how do you defend it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hilt, it is Google's." Or "Koin, it is simpler." No criteria, no reversibility.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Probability of KMP in 12 months? Hiring plan and Android seniority? Tolerance for runtime wiring crashes? Is build time already painful? Do we need per-user scopes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable; first extract constructors (constructor injection everywhere), which makes any framework a mechanical change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Hilt: best default for a pure Android app with juniors joining; (b) Koin + verify() + compiler plugin if KMP is likely; (c) manual AppContainer if only 14 screens and no scoping needs; (d) red herring: startup micro-benchmarks.
  4. How I'd verify: Spike one feature in each option; measure build delta (--scan), Macrobenchmark cold start, and error-message quality on an injected missing binding.
  5. Root cause (of the decision): The choice is about failure mode and reversibility, not features.
  6. Fix (recommendation): Constructor injection plus Hilt if no KMP commitment; if KMP is likely, Koin (or kotlin-inject/Metro after evaluation) with a verification test in CI. Keep framework use at the edges so a swap is cheap.
  7. Prevention: Write an ADR with the criteria and a revisit trigger (e.g., "KMP greenlit" or "build > 10 min").
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not adopt Metro on hype for a team this size; not build a bespoke DI framework; not mix two frameworks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CTO says KMP is happening in 3 months. -> Koin or Metro/kotlin-inject for shared code, keep Hilt out of commonMain.
  • Hilt build time hurts at 18 min clean. -> Use KSP, check aggregating tasks; consider build scans before blaming DI.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite startup picked Hilt, adopted KMP a year later, and ran Hilt on Android with a shared interface layer, paying a bridging tax they could have avoided with a 1-day spike.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: preference without criteria.
  • Hire: criteria-driven pick with the KMP and safety considerations.
  • Strong hire: reversible design, spike plan, ADR with revisit triggers.

questions.contextHtml: A 3M-DAU shopping app with 40 modules is on Koin 3.x and wants Hilt (leadership wants build-time safety after 3 wiring crashes in a quarter, about 0.15% crash-free-session loss). Constraints: weekly release train, staged rollout at 1%/10%/50%/100%, no feature freeze, 25 engineers. A big-bang PR was estimated at 6 weeks and unreviewable.
questions.promptHtml: How do you migrate without breaking live traffic?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace all module {} with @Module in one branch." Or never defines how both can coexist.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the real goal safety? (If yes, verify() + compiler plugin may be cheaper.) Which modules are leaves? KMP plans? Is Koin used as locator in places?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add verify() tests and ViewModel smoke tests now; this cuts the crash risk while migration is debated.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) incremental migration by feature with both containers alive is feasible; (b) hidden KoinComponent/get() usages are the hard part; (c) scopes (user session) need redesign; (d) red herring: build-time worries, which are measurable per module.
  4. How I'd verify: Grep/Konsist count of KoinComponent, inject(), getKoin; module dependency graph to pick leaf-first order; track --scan build time per step.
  5. Root cause: Not applicable; the risk is dual-container drift (same type created twice, duplicate singletons).
  6. Fix (plan): Phase 0: constructor-ify classes, remove locator calls. Phase 1: Hilt enabled in :app with a bridge: Hilt module provides objects obtained from Koin (@Provides fun api(): Api = getKoin().get()) or the reverse, never defining the same singleton in both. Phase 2: migrate leaf feature modules, deleting their Koin modules, each behind normal release trains. Phase 3: move shared singletons to Hilt, remove Koin bridge. Per-user scope becomes a custom component or a session holder.
  7. Prevention: Konsist rule banning new Koin imports after cutover; a test asserting each singleton type is declared in exactly one container; crash-free monitoring per staged rollout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not big-bang; not duplicate singletons; not migrate scope-heavy session code first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two feature teams still ship daily to Koin modules. -> Freeze new Koin modules by convention; allow Koin leaf edits until their turn.
  • What if the app later goes KMP? -> Shared code stays framework-free; DI wiring remains in platform source sets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite migration stalled for months at a duplicated OkHttpClient singleton in both containers, doubling connection pools and cache dirs until a single-owner rule was enforced.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang rewrite.
  • Hire: incremental with a bridge and leaf-first ordering.
  • Strong hire: questions the goal, adds verification first, single-owner invariant, enforcement and rollout metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
CI for an app using Koin 3.5 is flaky: about 8% of runs fail, always in the unit test module, with KoinAppAlreadyStartedException or tests passing alone but failing in the suite, and one test asserting against a repository mock from a previous test. Local runs pass 100% with --tests filters. Gradle runs tests in parallel forks with maxParallelForks = 4.

class CartTest : KoinTest {
    @Before fun setup() {
        startKoin { modules(appModule, module { single<Api> { mockApi } }) }
    }
    // no @After
}

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add retries." Or "rerun until green." Misses global state.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do tests use KoinTestRule? Are tests in the same JVM sharing GlobalContext? Are there parallel tests inside one JVM (JUnit parallel) or only forks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add @After { stopKoin() } to the offending classes to stabilise CI today.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) startKoin without stopKoin leaves the global container; the next test sees old overrides; (b) parallel tests inside one JVM share GlobalContext; (c) module override order; (d) red herring: forks, which isolate JVMs and cannot share Koin state.
  4. How I'd verify: Run the suite in random order, check GlobalContext.getOrNull() in @Before; run with --tests per class to confirm isolation.
  5. Root cause: Koin's default container is a process-global singleton; tests that start it without stopping leak both the container and mock bindings across test classes.
  6. Fix: Use KoinTestRule (koin-test-junit4), or isolated koinApplication, or better: construct classes by hand with fakes, no container.
class CartTest : KoinTest {
    @get:Rule val koinRule = KoinTestRule.create {
        modules(appModule, module { single<Api> { FakeApi() } })   // later definition overrides (verify allowOverride semantics for your version)
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Konsist/lint rule: unit tests for ViewModels and use cases must not start Koin; one verify() test and a few integration tests only; disable JUnit intra-JVM parallelism for Koin tests.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not retries that hide the leak; not overrideModules everywhere when constructor injection of fakes works.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Instrumented tests: how do you swap bindings? -> Custom test Application that starts Koin with test modules, or a custom runner.
  • Why is this less of a problem in Hilt? -> Hilt test components are generated per test, so state is isolated by design.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team cut a 12-minute suite flake problem to near zero by deleting 80% of Koin-in-unit-tests and passing fakes through constructors.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries.
  • Hire: global state diagnosis and stopKoin/KoinTestRule.
  • Strong hire: removes the container from unit tests, defines a test-boundary policy and enforces it.
